e01.abstract.existence.TorusEuler.theorem11: The theorem chooses a single smooth, odd, divergence-free periodic datum and a maximal Euler solution from it. The same velocity stays bounded while the magnitude of its curl at the origin tends to infinity at a finite positive time. The proof takes the existence part of `Paper.theorem_1_1`, whose statement also includes uniqueness among maximal velocities from that datum.

e01.abstract.bounded-velocity.TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness: One finite constant $C$ bounds the essential supremum of $|u(t,x)|$ over the fundamental cube for every $0\le t<T_*$. This clause of `EulerSingularityWitness` concerns the same $u$ whose curl at the origin diverges. Theorem 1.1 supplies the datum and solution.

e01.abstract.central-vorticity.TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness: The curl clause of `EulerSingularityWitness` takes the norm of $\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)$ first, then lets $t$ approach $T_*$ from within $[0,T_*)$. For every prescribed level the norm eventually stays above that level, for the same velocity that has the uniform speed bound.

e01.abstract.off-origin.TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness: The final two clauses apply `HasOffOriginLimits` to both $u$ and `timeDerivative T u`. On each compact $K$ away from the torus origin, the field and its spatial derivatives through every specified order $m$ have uniform limits as $t\uparrow T_*$. The two applications therefore cover the velocity and its first time derivative separately.
e01.abstract.off-origin.TorusEuler.HasOffOriginLimits: `HasOffOriginLimits` concerns one field. For each order $m$ and compact set $K$ disjoint from the integer lattice, it requires a $C^m$ limit field on an open neighborhood of $K$ and uniform convergence on $K$ of the spatial derivatives through order $m$. The witness applies this condition twice, to the velocity and its time derivative.

e01.intro.goal.TorusEuler.theorem11: The paper’s sentence asserts finite-time blow-up from smooth periodic initial data. The formal theorem additionally chooses odd divergence-free data, proves bounded velocity and central vorticity divergence, gives both divergent time integrals, and supplies every off-origin spatial limit. These are stronger conclusions for the same selected solution; they do not apply to every smooth initial datum.

e01.torus.cell.TorusEuler.centeredCell: The formal domain is the closed cube $[-1/2,1/2]^3\subset\mathbb R^3$, with Lebesgue measure. It is the same fundamental cell used in the paper. Opposite faces are identified by requiring the fields to be invariant under integer translations. The set defining the cube does not itself impose this condition. Including both faces does not change integrals or essential suprema, since the boundary has zero volume.

e01.torus.periodicity.TorusEuler.SpatiallyPeriodic: The paper identifies opposite faces of the unit cube. The formal statement uses fields on $\mathbb R^3$ invariant under every integer translation, which gives the same unit-torus representation. Periodicity imposes no regularity by itself.

e01.euler-equations.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution: The selected clauses are exactly $\partial_tu+D_xu\,u+\nabla p=0$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on $0\le t<T_*$. In the surrounding formal definition $u,p$ are smooth periodic fields with mean-zero pressure and $T_*>0$. Time differentiation is from within the interval, hence from the right at zero; these are the classical solution conventions used in the paper.

r5-root-introduction-scope.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_1_1: The formal theorem constructs smooth odd divergence-free data with bounded velocity and central vorticity divergence, and also gives every spatial derivative limit on compact sets away from the origin. These precise conclusions support the paper’s description of concentrated growth; they do not assert that vorticity is supported only at the origin. The theorem additionally gives maximality and both divergent time integrals.

r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_1_1: `EulerSingularityWitness` packages all the assertions in the printed theorem for one datum $u_0$, time $T_*$ and solution $u,p$. The last quantifier then ranges over any maximal solution from that same datum and requires equality of its lifespan and its velocity on $[0,T_*)$. That quantifier spells out the classical uniqueness used in the paper.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_1_1: The numbered Lean theorem provides one smooth odd datum and one maximal periodic solution for every part of the passage. The common endpoint $T_*$ governs both divergent integrals, the bounded-speed and central-curl pair, and the spatial limits of $u$ and $\partial_tu$. It also proves equality of lifespan and velocity for any other maximal solution from the chosen datum.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.IsMaximalEulerSolution: `IsMaximalEulerSolution` first requires a smooth periodic Euler solution on $[0,T_*)$. It then rules out a smooth Euler solution on every longer interval whose velocity agrees with $u$ throughout $[0,T_*)$. The existence and uniqueness assertions in Theorem 1.1 use this definition as a condition on a candidate solution.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution.velocity_eq_o: Give the theorem two smooth periodic Euler solutions with the same initial velocity. It proves that their velocities agree for every $0\le t<\min(T_1,T_2)$, the interval on which both are defined. Theorem 1.1 combines this agreement with maximality to compare their lifespans.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness: `EulerSingularityWitness` groups the hypotheses and conclusions about the chosen $u_0,T_*,u,p$. Joint smoothness is part of being a maximal classical solution, and $u(t,-x)=-u(t,x)$ is a separate clause. For that same $u$ it requires both infinite time integrals, a single speed bound, central curl tending to infinity, and off-origin spatial limits for $u$ and $\partial_tu$.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution: `IsEulerSolution` takes $T_*$ to be a real number and requires $T_*>0$. This gives a positive finite endpoint whenever the condition holds. The remaining fields require the Euler equations and joint smoothness on the half-open interval, with periodic velocity and mean-zero periodic pressure.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.HasOffOriginLimits: `HasOffOriginLimits` translates the compact-set clause into a statement about a supplied field on the periodic lift. For each $K$ avoiding $\mathbb Z^3$ and each $m$, there is a local $C^m$ limit on a neighborhood of $K$, and convergence on $K$ is uniform for every spatial derivative up to order $m$. The main witness separately supplies the condition for $u$ and for $\partial_tu$.

e01.remark.smooth-extension.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.remark_1_2: Both statements assert that a solution satisfying all of Theorem 1.1 can be chosen with a smooth space-time extension through $T_*$ away from the torus origin. The formal statement also makes the maximal-solution uniqueness explicit. It requires no Euler equation after $T_*$, and does not quantify over every singular Euler solution.
e01.remark.smooth-extension.TorusEuler.Paper.remark_1_2: The formal theorem proves the existential extension assertion for a solution with all of Theorem 1.1’s properties. Its extension need not solve Euler after $T_*$. This matches the remark. The stronger extension for all real times used in the auxiliary construction is a sufficient input, not an additional claim of the quoted sentence.

r2a1.intro.smooth-extension-proof-route.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.remark_1_2: The paper directs the reader to the auxiliary note for the extension in Remark 1.2. The formal proof instead invokes an auxiliary existence theorem that chooses one exponent and threshold, then a solution with a smooth extension. This suffices for the existential remark. It does not prove the broader auxiliary statement for every threshold satisfying the note’s additional bounds.

e01.intro.approximate-sequence.TorusEuler.paperTheorem71: The introduction asserts existence of smooth approximate solutions with vanishing residuals. The formal theorem chooses one admissible frequency schedule and constructs smooth odd periodic divergence-free velocities with the uniform bound $|R_j|\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$, together with support, increment and crossing estimates. The frequency schedule diverges, so the residual bound implies the quoted convergence. The theorem provides additional properties for the same sequence.
e01.intro.approximate-sequence.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: The paper asserts existence of the sequence. The formal condition lists properties required of a given construction, including smoothness and the residual bound $|R_j|\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$ on its stage interval. It does not construct a sequence or, by itself, prove that the frequencies diverge. The separate existence theorem supplies a construction satisfying it.

e01.intro.spatial-convergence.TorusEuler.PaperLimitAgreement: The paper asserts that the constructed sequence converges in spatial $C^m$ uniformly before $T_*$. This linked condition requires the stronger spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ convergence for given fields, also requires uniform velocity convergence through the accumulation time, and records agreement with any maximal solution. It does not assert existence of fields satisfying those requirements. Its accumulation time is not yet asserted to equal the maximal lifespan.
e01.intro.spatial-convergence.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStages.paper_pr: The visible statement assumes an inductive sequence, $\lambda_0\ge2$, activation times tending to $T>0$, and every stage defined through $T$. It supplies a smooth periodic Euler limit with spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ convergence uniformly on $[0,S]$ for every $S<T$ and every nonnegative integer $m$, and uniform velocity convergence through $T$. This is stronger convergence than the quoted $C^m$ assertion, but the sequence is assumed and equality of $T$ with the maximal lifespan is established later. The assumed sequence carries the frequency and order schedule of Theorem 7.1, activation times with $0\le t_{j+1}-t_j\le\tau_j$, and smooth odd divergence-free periodic $U_j$ on $[0,S_j]$ with $\|U_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_j$, Fourier support in $|k|\le2\lambda_j^5$, $\|R_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$, $\|O_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_j^{-1}$, $\|U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\lambda_j^{-1}$ for $m\le q_j$, $O_j=0$ before $t_j$ for $j\ge2$, and $O_j$ supported within $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ of the integer lattice. The spatial norm is the sum of supremum and one-half Hölder seminorms through order $m$.

e01.intro.localized-small-waves.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: The selected clauses require the oscillation at stage $j$ to be supported within distance $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ of the integer lattice and bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1}$ throughout the stage interval. This quantifies localization and small velocity, and is stronger in time than smallness only initially. The linked object is a condition on an existing construction, however; these clauses do not by themselves construct successively higher-frequency waves.

e01.intro.finite-growth-time.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: For a given construction, the formal condition requires activation times $t_j$ tending to a finite positive $T$, with $T<S_j$ for every stage. Together with its monotonicity clauses, this gives a finite sum of successive activation intervals. The condition itself does not assert existence of those times and does not say that the overlapping lengths $S_j-t_j$ have this sum. This is the precise interpretation of the introductory growth intervals.

r2a1.intro.wave.background.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: The paper assumes smooth $D$ with zero trace and symmetric $D'+D^2$. The formal theorem retains trace and symmetry but requires only a time derivative on an interval with unique relative derivatives. It proves the Euler identity under this weaker background regularity. The profile and wave hypotheses remain necessary.

r2a1.intro.wave.velocity.TorusEuler.affineWaveVelocity: The paper defines the perturbation $w=\mathbf aF(k\cdot x)$ and requires $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$. The formal formula defines the full velocity $u=Dx+w$ on $\mathbb R^3$ and imposes no transversality. Subtracting $Dx$ gives the displayed perturbation; perpendicularity is a separate assumption.
r2a1.intro.wave.velocity.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: The paper introduces a transverse plane-wave ansatz. The formal theorem uses that ansatz as an input and proves the Euler equations after also assuming the two wave equations, differentiability of $F$, $P'=F$, zero trace and symmetric $D'+D^2$. It is the theorem using the formula, rather than a definition of $w$.

intro.affine-euler.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: For $\operatorname{tr}D=0$, symmetric $D'+D^2$, transverse wave data and the two equations (1.4), the formal theorem proves the same Euler identity with the displayed pressure. It requires only differentiable $F$ and $P'=F$, omitting the paper’s smoothness, oddness and periodicity assumptions. Time derivatives are relative to an interval with unique derivatives.

intro.affine-equations.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.WaveOn: On a specified time interval $J$, the formal condition requires $k_t=-D^Tk$ and $\mathbf a_t=-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ at every time in $J$. These are exactly the displayed evolution equations with the coefficient substituted. Derivatives are taken within $J$, hence one-sided at included endpoints. The condition alone imposes neither $k\ne0$ nor $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$; those are separate wave hypotheses. Its quotient is assigned zero at $k=0$, a case excluded in the introductory wave.
intro.affine-equations.TorusEuler.affineWavePressureCoeff: The paper displays two differential equations and the pressure coefficient. This formal definition supplies only $p_{\rm w}=2k\cdot D\mathbf a/|k|^2$; it does not assert either evolution equation. The quotient is assigned zero at $k=0$, whereas the introductory wave has $k\ne0$.

intro.affine-pressure.TorusEuler.affineWavePressure: With $S=D'+D^2$, the formal formula is $-x\cdot Sx/2-p_{\rm w}P(k\cdot x)$, the same pressure. It is a definition. The facts that $S$ is symmetric and $P'=F$ are imposed when its gradient is used.

intro.self-advection.TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection: The formal statement proves the same cancellation for any $k,\mathbf a,x$ with $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$, assuming only that $F$ is differentiable at $k\cdot x$. The paper’s smooth odd periodic profile and time-dependent wave equations are unnecessary for this pointwise spatial identity.

r2a1.intro.phase-and-pressure-cancellati.TorusEuler.affineWave_materialAccelerati: The paper states phase transport and cancellation of the remaining acceleration by wave pressure. The formal statement gives only the acceleration formula $(D'+D^2)x+(\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a)F$, assuming phase transport and transversality. It does not itself state the pressure cancellation or the separate phase identity.
r2a1.intro.phase-and-pressure-cancellati.TorusEuler.hasGradientAt_affineWavePress: The formal statement proves $\nabla p=-Sx-p_{\rm w}F(k\cdot x)k$ for symmetric $S$ and $P'=F$ at the phase. The paper’s cancellation follows after taking $S=D'+D^2$ and using $\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a=p_{\rm w}k$; neither the wave equation nor phase transport is a conclusion of this spatial identity.

intro.pressure-transversality.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_affineWavePa: The paper asserts preservation of perpendicularity along an interval. The formal statement proves only the pointwise derivative identity $(k\cdot\mathbf a)'=0$ from the wave equations and $k\ne0$, without assuming an initial zero pairing. To obtain preservation one must apply the identity throughout an interval and use $k(t_0)\cdot\mathbf a(t_0)=0$.

intro.origin-gradient.TorusEuler.hasFDerivAt_planeWave: The paper gives the central gradient under $F'(0)=1$. The formal statement proves $\nabla w(x)=F'(k\cdot x)\mathbf a\otimes k$ at every phase where $F$ is differentiable. Substitution of $x=0$ and the normalization yields the paper’s formula; no periodicity or wave equation is needed.

intro.preceding-frame.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame: The paper defines the three frame vectors and the time-dependent strength $\sigma=|k_p||\mathbf a_p|$. This formal definition gives the frame vectors only. For nonzero perpendicular data it is the same oriented orthonormal frame; normalization at a zero vector is defined as zero.
intro.preceding-frame.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: The paper’s $\sigma$ in this introductory display varies with time. The formal definition is the frozen value $|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|$ at activation. It agrees with the display only at $t=t_0$; it is the later frozen parameter of Section 2.2.1.

intro.preceding-shear.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r: For nonzero preceding data and a nonzero time scale $r$, the formal identity is $S(\sigma_p(t)/\sigma_p(0))E_2\otimes E_1=r^{-1}\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p$, where $S=\sigma_p(0)/r$. Multiplying by $r$ gives the paper’s rank-one identity. It is an identity of linear maps; identifying it with the wave’s central gradient also uses $F\prime(0)=1$.

intro.two-coupling-frame.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.movingFrameDeriva:
The paper’s two-entry model gives $E_1'=-
u E_2$, $E_2'=
u E_1-\eta E_3$, $E_3'=\eta E_2$. For nonzero transverse wave data over a trace-free background, the formal theorem also allows $B_{13}
e0$ and gives the corresponding extra terms, together with $(\log\sigma)'=B_{33}$. Setting $B_{13}=0$ recovers the quoted equations.

intro-amplification-polarization.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteComparison: The paper selects the direction $E_2-\sqrt{2\nu/\sigma}E_1$. The formal theorem assumes the particular representative $\mathbf a(t_0)=E_2-E_1/S$, which is the same direction since $S=\sqrt{\sigma/(2\nu)}$. This is an input to its comparison conclusions. The theorem does not prove the separate assertion that the direction is asymptotically growing.

r2a1.intro.strong-shear-factor.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: In the exact two-entry shear model, with $\varepsilon$ and the normalized interval fixed, the $(1,2)$ coefficient of the limiting amplitude matrix is $\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)$, where $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. Undoing the normalization multiplies it by $r/S=2\nu$. The formal assertion gives the finite-$S$ equations and uniform convergence of all entries under the exact-model hypotheses.
r2a1.intro.strong-shear-factor.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_3: In the exact two-entry shear model, with $\varepsilon$ and the normalized interval fixed, the $(1,2)$ coefficient of the limiting amplitude matrix is $\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)$, where $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. Undoing the normalization multiplies it by $r/S=2\nu$. The formal assertion gives the finite-$S$ equations and uniform convergence of all entries under the exact-model hypotheses.

intro-amplification-gain.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteReturn: Let $A$ be the actual maximum amplitude of the prescribed wave on the full normalized interval $[0,T]$. In the growing launch direction, under the small coefficient-error and successor-ratio hypotheses, the theorem bounds every amplitude at $0\le\tau\le1$ by $e^{3-1/\sqrt\varepsilon}A$. At $\tau=0$ this gives the amplification factor $A/|\mathbf a(t_0)|\ge e^{-3}e^{1/\sqrt\varepsilon}$. The reference slope solving its own equation is a supplied input.

intro-amplification-new-frame.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame: For nonzero perpendicular $k,\mathbf a$, the three vectors are exactly $\widehat k,\widehat a,\widehat k\times\widehat a$. The definition itself accepts zero or nonperpendicular data; then it need not be an orthonormal frame. The paper’s wave hypotheses supply the nonzero transverse setting.

intro-amplification-new-couplings.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry: The formal entry of a linear map $D$ in a triple $E$ is $E_i\cdot DE_j$. Choosing the first or third vector for $i$ and the second for $j$ gives the two displayed couplings. The definition supplies neither positivity nor orthonormality; those come from the wave and coupling assumptions.

intro-amplification-cancellation.TorusEuler.referenceCouplingNumerators: The paper describes a late-time cancellation between large terms. The formal result proves two polynomial identities under $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, $(1+x^2)s^2=1$ and $Y=s(1+e)-\varepsilon\tau xs^2/2$. They give the reduced numerators, but contain no late-time size comparison. The angle substitution $x=\tan\varphi$, $s=\cos\varphi$ and bounds on $e$ supply that interpretation.

intro-amplification-late-angle.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_7: The angle in the formal estimate is the reference $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. It is used to estimate the couplings computed in the actual successor frame from $M$ and the new wave. The introductory phrase defines an angle from the actual wave direction, so equality with the reference angle would need a separate argument.
intro-amplification-late-angle.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_7: The angle in the formal estimate is the reference $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$. It is used to estimate the couplings computed in the actual successor frame from $M$ and the new wave. The introductory phrase defines an angle from the actual wave direction, so equality with the reference angle would need a separate argument.

intro-amplification-crossing.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteReturn: For the growing launch direction and small coefficient error, take $0<\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ and $H=2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}\le T$. The theorem supplies a zero $\tau_m$ of the reference slope with $2\le\varepsilon\tau_m\le3$ and a crossing strictly between $\tau_m$ and $H$. It measures strength at every crossing in the closed interval against the actual maximum amplitude on $[0,T]$. The reference zero and the actual maximum enter different parts of the conclusion.

e01.initial-shear.formula.TorusEuler.stationaryShear: For every real $\rho$, the formal formula is $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$ on $\mathbb R^3$, where $e_1,e_2,e_3$ are the coordinate vectors. It is odd and invariant under integer translations, so it represents the stated torus field. Positivity and smallness of $\rho$ are imposed for amplification, not by this formula. The Euler equation with zero pressure is established by a separate theorem.

e01.initial-shear.euler.TorusEuler.isEulerSolution_stationaryShe: The paper uses $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$ with a small positive $\rho$. The formal theorem verifies the same stationary Euler solution with zero pressure for every real $\rho$ on every positive lifespan. The restrictions on $\rho$ belong to the later amplification step.

e01.initial-shear.couplings.TorusEuler.stationaryShearGradient_origi: The paper gives two numerical coupling values and their ratio. This result identifies the derivative of the stationary shear at the origin with its stated linear map. It does not itself evaluate either coupling or their ratio.
e01.initial-shear.couplings.TorusEuler.stationaryShearGradient_coupl: For every real $\rho$, the formal statement gives the two coordinate entries $2\pi$ and $2\pi\rho$ of the specified shear-gradient map. It does not identify that map with the derivative or state $\eta/\nu=\rho$. The derivative identity and division by $2\pi\ne0$ complete the paper’s sentence; positivity requires $\rho>0$.

e01.initial-shear.flow.TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow: The paper says the explicit flow supplies the first wave. The formal definition gives $X(t,a)=a+t\sin(2\pi a_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$, the stationary-shear flow, but does not construct the first localized wave or prove its launch properties. Those require the later first-wave statements.

localized.intro.periodic-localization.TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile: The formal formula periodizes $a\mapsto f(t,a,k\cdot a)$ on the centred unit cell and composes it with a supplied map $A(t,x)$. It expresses the periodization and change to particle labels described in the paper. It assumes neither that $A$ is transported by the parent velocity nor that $f$ is smooth and supported away from the cell boundary, so those parts of the quoted construction require separate hypotheses.

localized.intro.real-wave-vector.TorusEuler.localizedCompletedWave_proper: The formal theorem permits any real $k\in\mathbb R^3$, with no integer-lattice restriction. It obtains a smooth periodic divergence-free completed wave from a smooth lattice-equivariant label map and a potential vanishing in a strip near every face of the centred cell. Nonzero transported phase gradient and transversality are also required. The support condition is exactly what permits this use of a nonintegral wave vector.

c8-endpoint-choice-introduction.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2: For a smooth periodic divergence-free parent on $[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$, with $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)\le I$, the formal statement solves the forced endpoint problem with $z(0)=z(T)=0$. Since the physical displacement is $\xi=(D_aX)z$, this fixes final particle positions to first order. It selects the initial correction for a smooth force. It does not prescribe a nonlinear perturbed flow with exactly the same final positions.

e01.endpoint.flow-equation.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn: The formal flow equations are $X(s,s,a)=a$ and $\partial_tX(s,t,a)=u(t,X(s,t,a))$ for $s,t$ in the given interval. Setting $s=0$ gives the paper's $X(t,a)$. At interval endpoints the derivative is taken within the interval. These equations define what it means to be a flow. This declaration does not assert existence or regularity.

e01.endpoint.first-variation-equation.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_endpointDisp: The paper defines $\xi$ by varying the particle flow and obtains both its differential equation and $\xi(0)=0$. The formal theorem assumes $F_t=MF$, $z_t=v$ and sets $\xi=Fz$, proving only $\xi_t=M\xi+Fv$. Taking $F=D_aX$ and $Fv=b\circ X$ gives the displayed derivative equation; initial vanishing and the interpretation as a variation of flows are not conclusions of this theorem.
e01.endpoint.first-variation-equation.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: The paper's unknown is the physical trajectory displacement $\xi$. The formal definition instead specifies smooth periodic label fields with $z_t=v$, $B=Fv$ and $z(0)=z(T)=0$, together with the forced mean equation. Putting $\xi=Fz$ and $b=B\circ X^{-1}$ yields (1.5) by a product rule. It describes an endpoint solution, rather than proving the first-variation expansion for $X_\delta$.

r2a1.intro.initial-displacement.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: The formal condition is $z(T,a)=0$, where $z$ is the label displacement. The physical variation is $\xi(T,a)=F(T,a)z(T,a)$ with $F=D_aX$ invertible, so the condition is equivalent to $\xi(T,a)=0$. It is imposed in the definition of a smooth mean solution. It is not derived from the common initial positions.

e01.endpoint.selected-initial-value.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: The paper says the endpoint condition selects an initial correction. For $0<T\le1$, the formal theorem compares two already existing smooth periodic mean solutions for the same parent and forcing, both with $z(0)=z(T)=0$, and proves equality of $B=Fz_t$ throughout the interval. Its parent assumptions include $H^\#\le I$ and bounds on $F^{-1}$ and $M$. This proves uniqueness of the initial correction, but existence comes from the endpoint inverse.

e01.endpoint.linearized-euler.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse_smooth_for: For a smooth periodic force $f$, supply the label force $f\circ X$ to the endpoint inverse. The theorem forms the physical correction $b=(Fz_t)\circ X^{-1}$. Along a particle path, time differentiation becomes $\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla$, and the Piola identity makes $b$ divergence free. The parent is allowed to have a momentum residual.

e01.endpoint.pressure-cancellation.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.det_labelDeriva: The paper cancels the pressure term in the displacement energy using both volume preservation and a divergence constraint. For a jointly $C^2$ periodic divergence-free velocity, this formal theorem proves only $\det D_aX=1$. This is the needed Jacobian identity. It does not state the vanishing of the pressure pairing.
e01.endpoint.pressure-cancellation.TorusEuler.integral_inner_gradient_cente: The paper's pressure term is written along particle trajectories. The formal theorem proves $\int_{\mathbb T^3}w\cdot\nabla q=0$ for $C^1$ periodic $w,q$ with $\operatorname{div}w=0$. To obtain the displacement cancellation, one must choose $w=\xi\circ X^{-1}$ and change variables using volume preservation. Those geometric steps are not part of this theorem.

e01.endpoint.poincare-local.TorusEuler.terminal_poincare_pointwise: The paper bounds $|\xi(t,a)|^2$ by $(T-t)\int_t^T|\xi_\tau|^2$. For a continuously differentiable path with $\xi(T)=0$, the formal theorem's conclusion has the larger integral $\int_0^T|\xi_\tau|^2$. Its proof contains the paper's sharper tail-integral estimate before enlarging the interval. Thus the selected proof establishes the displayed step, but the declared bound is weaker at $t>0$.

e01.endpoint.coercivity.TorusEuler.endpointDisplacementEnergy_co: For a $C^1$ path with $\xi(T)=0$ and continuous $H\le I$, the formal theorem proves the factor $1-T^2/2$ in a time integral along one path. The paper's formula integrates over both time and label and also uses $T\le1$ for the factor $1/2$. Integration over labels and that final numerical specialization are not conclusions of this declaration.
e01.endpoint.coercivity.TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_coercive: The formal theorem assumes $F_t=MF$, $z_t=v$, both endpoint values of $z$ zero, continuous derivatives and $0\le T\le1$. It proves the one-half bound for the label energy along one path, with $\xi=Fz$ and $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)\le I$. It does not itself state the space-time norm in (1.9) or the preceding factor $1-T^2/2$.

r2a1.intro.hessian-upper.TorusEuler.endpointDisplacementEnergy_co: Let $T\ge0$, let $\xi:[0,T]\to E$ have a continuous derivative and $\xi(T)=0$, and let $H(t)$ be a continuous bounded-linear-operator family on a real Hilbert space $E$. If $\langle H(t)w,w\rangle\le\|w\|^2$ for every $t,w$, the formal statement gives $\int_0^T(\|\xi_t\|^2-\langle H\xi,\xi\rangle)\,dt\ge(1-T^2/2)\int_0^T\|\xi_t\|^2\,dt$. It needs neither symmetry of $H$ nor $\xi(0)=0$. The paper integrates this one-path bound over particle labels and uses $T\le1$ to obtain the factor $1/2$.

r2a1.intro.zero-source-uniqueness.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: The paper discusses the kernel of the linearized map from initial velocity to final physical displacement. The formal theorem does not define that map: it proves equality of the pulled-back physical means of two smooth solutions with the same parent, forcing and two zero label endpoints on the same $[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$. Comparing a homogeneous solution with zero gives the relevant trivial-kernel conclusion after $\xi=Fz$ and $b=B\circ X^{-1}$ are identified.

e01.endpoint.approximate-hessian.TorusEuler.endpointHessian_eq_pressureHe: With $M=D_xU\circ X$, the formal theorem proves $-(M_t+M^2)=(D_x^2p_U-D_xR_U)\circ X$. It assumes joint $C^2$ regularity of $U$, the trajectory equation and differentiability of the pressure gradient at the point considered. The residual is the actual momentum defect of $U,p_U$, and time derivatives are taken within $[0,T]$. The parent need not solve Euler and the effective Hessian need not be symmetric.

e01.endpoint.quantitative-inverse.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse: The theorem gives polynomial control of both the instantaneous projected inverse and the endpoint velocity norm. The polynomial uses bounds on the inverse deformation, strain, and the kinetic and vorticity coefficients and their first derivatives. The matrix fields may be supplied directly with the stated identities, including the quadratic-form bound, and the coefficient norms use suprema.

localized.intro.affine-pressure-hessian.TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian:
The paper's affine formula permits any primitive $P'=F$. The formal theorem uses the selected $P_h$, $0<h\le1$, but allows a variable $C^2$ coefficient $c(x)$ and phase $	heta(x)$. Its Hessian includes the leading term $-cF_h'(	heta)
abla	heta\otimes
abla	heta$ and terms involving $
abla c,D^2c,D^2	heta$. Constant $c=p_{m w}$ and linear $	heta=k\cdot x$ recover the paper's formula for the chosen family, not for arbitrary $F$.

localized.intro.profile-slopes.TorusEuler.hasDerivAt_waveProfile_zero: For $0<h\le1$, this formal theorem proves only $F_h'(0)=1$ for the constructed family. The paper's display also contains the inequalities $-Ch\le F_h'\le1$ at every phase. Those bounds are supplied by the other linked theorem, rather than by this normalization result.
localized.intro.profile-slopes.TorusEuler.deriv_waveProfile_bounds: For $0<h\le1$ and every phase, this formal theorem proves $-h/2\le F_h'\le1$, specifying $C=1/2$ in the paper's bound. It does not state the separate central identity $F_h'(0)=1$ in the same display. Thus it strengthens the quantitative slope clause but covers only that clause. The normalization is established separately.

localized.intro.central-plane-gradient.TorusEuler.hasFDerivAt_planeWave: The formal theorem computes the derivative of $x\mapsto\mathbf aF(k\cdot x)$ at any point where the scalar derivative exists: it is $F'(k\cdot x)\mathbf a\otimes k$. The paper uses only $x=0$ and $F_h'(0)=1$, which give the displayed central gradient. No periodicity, smoothness away from that point or nonzero wave vector is needed for this local derivative formula.

localized.intro.positive-curvature.TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u: For $0<h\le1$ and $p_{\rm w}\ge0$, the formal theorem gives $v\cdot[-p_{\rm w}F_h'(s)\,k\otimes k]v\le(h/2)p_{\rm w}|k|^2|v|^2$ for every vector $v$. This controls the positive eigenvalue in (1.11) with $C=1/2$ for the constructed family, including the zero coefficient. It bounds the upper side of the rank-one Hessian. It does not bound its absolute operator norm by $O(h)$.

localized.intro.small-velocity.TorusEuler.norm_waveProfile_le: For every $0<h\le1$ and phase $s$, the formal theorem proves $|F_h(s)|\le h/2$. Consequently the affine-wave velocity $\mathbf aF_h(k\cdot x)$ has magnitude at most $h|\mathbf a|/2$. The paper states only the order $O(h|\mathbf a|)$. The formal bound specifies the constant for the chosen family and does not assert that its central gradient is small.

localized.intro.bump-construction.TorusEuler.waveSlope: The formal slope is the periodized bump $\psi(s/h)$ minus its phase mean $c_h$, divided by $1-c_h$. For the chosen bump and $0<h\le1$, $0\le c_h\le h/4$, so the denominator is positive and the negative part is shallow. The function defined here is the slope. The velocity profile is its integral from zero. Smoothness and the quantitative derivative bounds are proved elsewhere in the same construction.

e01.correction.frequency-truncation.TorusEuler.paperProposition511_physicalC: The formal theorem starts with a smooth periodic odd divergence-free approximate velocity and uses a smooth even Fourier multiplier equal to one on the unit ball and zero outside the ball of radius two, rescaled by $\Lambda\ge1$. It constructs the truncated child and controls the difference from the approximation, its new residual and its pressure Hessian. This is the truncation operation described here. The theorem assumes the approximate velocity has already been constructed.

e01.correction.parent-residual.TorusEuler.momentumResidual: The formal definition is $R_U=\partial_tU+(U\cdot\nabla)U+\nabla p_U$, using time derivatives within the prescribed parent interval. Thus $R_U$ is computed from the given velocity and pressure. It is not a freely chosen force. The definition alone imposes no incompressibility or smallness, and does not include frequency truncation; those are properties of the selected parent.

localized.intro.phase-trajectory.TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject: If $A(t,X(t,a))=a$, the formal theorem gives $f^\natural(t,X(t,a))=f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ for every profile $f$. Choosing $f(t,a,s)=s$ gives $\theta(t,X(t,a))=k_*\cdot a$. Thus it states a general evaluation identity containing the paper's phase formula. It assumes the inverse relation, without proving the flow equation or spatial periodicity of the phase.

localized.intro.phase-gradient.TorusEuler.hasGradientAt_transportedPhas: For a differentiable inverse label map $A$, the formal theorem proves $\nabla_x(k_*\cdot A)=(D_xA)^Tk_*$. At $x=X(t,a)$ this gives the paper's transported wave vector. It is a local chain rule and does not assume $k_*\ne0$ or that the phase is periodic.
localized.intro.phase-gradient.TorusEuler.labelWaveVector: The formal definition reads the derivative of the reverse flow at $X(t,a)$ and applies its transpose to $k_*$. Once the forward and reverse maps are established as inverses, this is $\kappa=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$. Nonvanishing follows from the smooth-flow inverse and $k_*\ne0$; it is not asserted by the formula alone.

localized.intro.slow-fast-derivatives.TorusEuler.transportedProfile_chainRule: If the inverse label map satisfies $A_t+D_xA\,U=0$ and the profile has the indicated joint derivatives, the formal statement splits $D_xf^\natural$ into $D_af\,D_xA$ and the phase term $(\partial_sf)\kappa^T$. It also gives $D_tf^\natural=\partial_tf$ at fixed label. This is the distinction described in the paper. It is a chain rule, not a bound on the relative sizes of these derivatives.

localized.intro.time-cutoff.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff: The formal definition requires a real cutoff smooth on $[0,T]$, valued in $[0,1]$ and zero for times in that interval before $t_0$. This describes later-wave activation but does not choose the constant-one first-wave cutoff or require eventual equality to one. Values outside $[0,T]$ are unrestricted.
localized.intro.time-cutoff.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.first: This formal construction chooses $t_0=0$ and $\widetilde\chi\equiv1$, giving the first-wave case of the sentence. It does not specify a cutoff for later waves. Its derivative is zero, so it contributes no activation residual.

localized.intro.level-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Zd: This formal definition gives $Z_p=V_p+C_p+B_p$, with the correction inherited from $V_{p-1}$. It states the second part of the display, not the identity for the full retained expansion. The finite-sum equality and the surviving term $C_{P+1}$ require the accompanying reindexing result.
localized.intro.level-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Cd: This declaration translates the stored correction index into the paper's $C_p$: the correction generated by $V_p$ is denoted $C_{p+1}$. It defines neither the complete $Z_p$ nor the expansion. At index zero subtraction is truncated. The paper uses indices at least one, with $C_1=0$ imposed separately.
localized.intro.level-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.expansion: The formal sum is $\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$. For $P\ge1$ and $C_1=0$, regrouping gives the paper's $\sum_{p=1}^PZ_p+C_{P+1}$. The stored corrections are indexed by the oscillations that generate them. This is a definition of a finite sum, without equations or estimates for its terms.
localized.intro.level-profile.TorusEuler.HierarchyProfiles.velocity_eq: For $P\ge1$ and $C_1=0$, the formal theorem proves exactly the reindexing $\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)=\sum_{p=1}^PZ_p+C_{P+1}$. It holds for arbitrary additive families. No convergence of an infinite expansion is asserted.

localized.intro.leading-level.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion: The formal definition of an admissible expansion requires $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$ on the centered label cell, its corresponding phase pressure, $C_1=0$ and $B_1=0$. Consequently $Z_1=V_1$. The leading wave uses the chosen radial envelope and profile $F_h$. This is a list of conditions on a supplied expansion, rather than an existence theorem.
localized.intro.leading-level.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr: The formal construction retains the supplied leading velocity and phase pressure and sets the first mean velocity and mean pressure to zero. It does not itself identify that supplied velocity with $\widetilde\chi A_1$, nor state $C_1=0$. Those identifications and the unused-index result are needed for the complete sentence.

At positive depth, the formal theorem sets all unused entries, including the stored correction at index zero, to zero. That entry is $C_1$ in paper notation. The result does not identify the leading velocity with the activated wave or prove the first-mean condition; those are separate parts of the construction.

localized.intro.level-scaling.TorusEuler.hierarchyOscExponent: The formal definition assigns exponent $-5/4-2(p-1)/3$ to the oscillatory level. Relative to level one, this is the factor $\lambda^{-2(p-1)/3}$ in the paper. It does not prove a norm bound for $Z_p$, $V_p$, $C_p$ or $B_p$, or account for the parent-dependent constants. Those claims require the hierarchy estimates.

localized.intro.phase-split.TorusEuler.phaseMean: The formal definition gives $\langle f\rangle_s=\int_0^1f(s)\,ds$ at fixed time and label. For $f=H_2$, this is the mean in the sentence. It does not itself define the oscillatory difference. Smoothness of the paper's profiles ensures that this integral is the ordinary phase average.
localized.intro.phase-split.TorusEuler.phaseOscillation: The formal definition gives the oscillatory part $f-\int_0^1f(s)\,ds$. With $f=H_2$, it is exactly the second term in the paper's split. For an integrable period-one profile its phase mean is zero; neither integrability nor periodicity is imposed merely by the definition.

e01.correction.mean-source.TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.level_two_: At level two, $C_1=B_1=0$ and the linear terms have zero phase average. Under the supplied identity for the average of $(C_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$, the theorem rewrites $-\langle H_2\rangle_s-R_U\circ X$ as the negative average of the remaining products minus the parent residual in label coordinates.
e01.correction.mean-source.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.meanSource: The formal definition prescribes the mean source as $-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R_U\circ X$. At $p=2$, this is precisely the force needed to cancel the averaged error and parent residual. The existence of a mean correction satisfying that equation comes from the endpoint inverse, not from this source formula.

e01.correction.mean-equation.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse_smooth_for: Apply the endpoint inverse to the physical force $-\langle H_2\rangle_s-R_U$, using its pullback by $X$ as the input. The theorem produces a smooth divergence-free correction with the strain term $(\nabla U)B_2$. The hierarchy must first supply smoothness and periodicity of this particular force.
e01.correction.mean-equation.TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.level_two_: This theorem calculates the source for the mean equation by averaging $H_2$ and including $-R_U\circ X$ at level two. Solving for the divergence-free $B_2$ and its pressure uses the endpoint inverse separately. The code here supplies the right-hand side of that solve.

e01.correction.mean-endpoints.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: The formal definition imposes $z(0)=z(T)=0$ and $z_t=v$ for label fields, with $B=Fv$. Thus $\xi=Fz$ has zero physical displacement at both endpoints. This states the first-order endpoint requirement. It does not prove that a solution or an initial value realizing it exists.
e01.correction.mean-endpoints.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: Under the same smooth parent and forcing on $[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$, with $H^\#\le I$, the formal theorem proves equality of the physical means of any two endpoint solutions. Consequently $B_2(0)$ is unique. It compares existing solutions and must be combined with the inverse's existence result to justify the paper's selection claim.

localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr: The formal theorem organizes the mean and oscillatory equations for every retained level $2\le p\le P$, assuming their linear solvers and prescribed operations. At $p=2$ its source has the algebraic form in (1.12). It does not itself identify the abstract operations with physical derivatives or assert $\kappa\cdot V_2=0$ and $\langle V_2\rangle_s=0$. Those geometric constraints come from the supplied transverse solutions.
localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryPhaseSolve_: For continuous coefficients along a single particle label, a transported initially nonzero covector and a continuous period-one zero-mean force, the formal theorem constructs a zero-initial periodic transverse solution with normalized phase pressure. It proves the differential equation at each phase. It does not insert the particular source containing $H_2,B_2$, or prove its smooth dependence on labels, as required for the displayed spatial field.
localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.TransverseSolution: The formal definition requires $V_t+MV+\kappa\partial_s\pi=f$, transversality, zero phase mean and zero initial data, with normalized phase pressure. It therefore specifies the left side and constraints of (1.12) for a general source. It neither identifies the particular right side nor proves existence of such a solution.
localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion: An admissible expansion requires the transverse equation with its oscillatory and supplementary sources, with $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$ and $C_1=0$. At level two these sources give exactly (1.12), and the transverse-solution condition includes perpendicularity, zero phase mean and zero initial data. This is part of the definition of an admissible finite expansion; its existence is a separate theorem.
localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.suppSource: The formal definition supplies only the supplementary forcing $-\sum_{i=2}^p(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_{p+1-i}$. At $p=2$, $Y_1=V_1$ because $C_1=0$, so it becomes $-(B_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_s(\widetilde\chi A_1)$. The remaining source, differential equation and transverse constraints are not conclusions of this definition.

localized.intro.mean-fast-zero-average.TorusEuler.hierarchy_phaseMean_supplemen: At fixed time and label, the formal theorem proves $\int_0^1(B\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY\,ds=0$ when $B,\kappa$ are independent of phase and $Y$ is differentiable, period one, with continuous derivative. Taking $B=B_2$ and $Y=\widetilde\chi A_1$ gives the cancellation described here. The theorem does not provide the size estimate or level assignment of that source.

localized.intro.zero-start-correction.TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryPhaseSolve_: On a closed interval, the formal theorem solves $V_t+MV+\kappa\partial_s\pi=f$ with $V$ initially zero, periodic in phase, transverse and of zero phase mean. It assumes continuous coefficients, a transported initially nonzero covector, and a forcing continuous in the supremum norm on period-one zero-mean phase functions. This is the fixed-label amplitude solve described in the sentence. Constructing a smooth family over all particle labels is a further step.

localized.intro.exact-divergence-correct.TorusEuler.divergence_completedWaveOn: The formal theorem proves $\operatorname{div}(V^\natural+C[V]^\natural)=0$ on an open region where the inverse map and potential are $C^2$, the covector comes from that map and is nonzero, and $V$ is transverse. Taking $V=V_2$ gives the local cancellation. The paper uses a smooth periodic field on the torus, which additionally requires the extension from the label cell.
localized.intro.exact-divergence-correct.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion: The formal definition requires $C_3=C[V_2]$ and a transverse, zero-mean second oscillation. It specifies the correction used in the paper but does not itself prove divergence cancellation. That conclusion uses the geometric curl identities and regularity of the evaluated profiles.

localized.intro.next-level-completion.TorusEuler.hierarchy_completion_previous: The formal theorem gives the correction exponent from level $p-1$ as the oscillatory exponent at level $p$ minus $1/3$. At $p=3$, this explains why the correction of $V_2$ fits into level three. It is an equality between powers assigned to estimates. It does not prove an estimate for $C_3$ or construct the next mean and oscillatory solutions.

e01.correction.retained-completion.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.expansion: The formal definition retains $\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$, so $C_{P+1}$ is included as the correction generated by $V_P$. The sum is finite and empty at $P=0$. No convergence statement is involved.
e01.correction.retained-completion.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion: The formal expansion conditions impose $C_{p+1}=C[V_p]$ for $1\le p\le P$, while $V_{P+1}=B_{P+1}=0$. Thus the last divergence correction remains even though the next oscillation and mean are set to zero. These are conditions on an expansion, not a proof of its existence.
e01.correction.retained-completion.TorusEuler.HierarchyProfiles.velocity: The formal velocity sum stores each correction at the index of its generating oscillation. Therefore summing through stored index $P$ includes the paper's $C_{P+1}$. It defines the retained perturbation but does not yet add the parent or evaluate at the transported phase.

e01.correction.depth-remainder.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Trunc: For the truncated parent, a nonzero central wave with $\gamma\le1$, and $L^6\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, the theorem chooses a seed and then an expansion for each allowed cutoff and depth $P\ge2$. For that same expansion at every derivative order $n$, it gives $\|R_P\|_{[n]}\le C_{n,P}\lambda^{-5/4-2P/3}$. Each extra level contributes $\lambda^{-2/3}$ to this bound.
e01.correction.depth-remainder.TorusEuler.hierarchyOscExponent: The formal definition assigns $-5/4-2(p-1)/3$ to level $p$. Substitution $p=P+1$ gives $-5/4-2P/3$, identifying the factor in the paper. This is arithmetic only: it does not prove that a remainder has that size or state the required lower bound on frequency relative to the parent.

e01.correction.approximate-velocity.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Physi: For a smooth periodic odd divergence-free parent and smooth periodic pressure, the formal theorem at depth $P\ge2$ proves that the constructed velocity, pressure and residual are smooth and periodic, that the velocity is divergence free, and that its actual Euler momentum residual equals the assembled residual. These are the approximate-solution properties described here. Bounds making that residual small are separate estimates.

For positive depth, this formal theorem states only the equality of the constructed velocity with the parent plus the leading wave, remaining oscillations and mean correction. It identifies the four terms, but does not by itself prove smoothness, incompressibility or the residual equation. Those conclusions are supplied by the added assembly theorem.

e01.correction.cutoff-error.TorusEuler.paperProposition511_physicalC: For $P\ge2$ and cutoff frequency $\Lambda\ge1$, the formal theorem bounds the $C_tC^{2,1/2}$ difference between the child and approximate velocities by $C_P\Lambda^{2-P}(1+\|V\|_{C_tC^{P,1/2}})^2$. It also controls the new residual and pressure-Hessian change. The exponent $2-P$ is an integer and is negative at $P>2$. This is the truncation error controlled by the frequency cutoff.

e01.correction.next-coercivity.TorusEuler.inductionPressure_endpointHes: Assume a jointly $C^2$ parent and a trajectory, frequencies with $\lambda_0\ge4$ and $\lambda_{n+1}\ge2\lambda_n$, a pressure-Hessian upper bound $\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i^{-1}I$, and $\|D_xR_U\|\le1/2$. The formal theorem concludes $H^\#\le I$ along that trajectory. It establishes the upper-curvature condition used for the next mean solve. The coercive energy estimate additionally uses the time bound $T\le1$ and endpoint conditions.

e01.correction.transported-support.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Physi: At depth $P\ge1$, suppose the leading profiles and their activation terms vanish before activation and outside one closed label set $S$. The formal theorem proves that the full oscillatory velocity vanishes at a point whenever its inverse-flow label is outside $S$ or the time precedes activation. It further identifies the residual there with interactions between means. The means themselves, and a later Fourier-truncation difference, need not have this support.

intro.pressure-not-control.TorusEuler.affineWavePressureCoeff: The formal definition gives $p_{\rm w}=2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)/|k|^2$. It does not derive this coefficient from a requirement of incompressibility or state that it is the only possible coefficient. At $k=0$ division is assigned zero, whereas the wave argument uses $k\ne0$.
intro.pressure-not-control.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_affineWavePa: At a time where $k\ne0$ and $k_t=-D^Tk$, $\mathbf a_t=-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$, the formal statement proves $(k\cdot\mathbf a)_t=0$. This is a derivative identity at that time. Preservation of transversality on an interval additionally uses this identity throughout the interval and an initial value $k(t_0)\cdot\mathbf a(t_0)=0$. The statement verifies the prescribed coefficient. It does not derive its uniqueness from incompressibility.

r5-root-central-gradient-setting.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: The formal condition records the central decomposition $D_xU_j(0)=D_xU_{j-1}(0)+\widetilde\chi_j\mathbf a_j\otimes\kappa_j+E_{c,j}$ with $\|E_{c,j}\|\le\lambda_j^{-1/4}$, together with regularity and increment bounds. It assumes no neighborhood of spatial linearity. It does not itself prove that corrections destroy linearity or provide every spatial-variation estimate invoked by the paper; those analytic steps lie in the construction.

e01.conventions.leray-projection.TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_sub_rea: The paper writes the spatial identity $\mathbb P=I-\nabla\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$. The formal theorem proves its equality of Fourier coefficients for real $L^2$ vector fields on the unit torus. The inverse Laplacian’s constant mode is zero, so constant velocity modes are retained. The coefficient identity is the Fourier formulation of the projection, rather than a pointwise classical identity for arbitrary fields.
e01.conventions.leray-projection.TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode: For a frequency $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ and vector coefficient $a$, the formal definition gives only the scalar multiplier $-2\pi i(k\cdot a)/(4\pi^2|k|^2)$ when $k\ne0$, with value zero at $k=0$. This is the scalar part $\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$ of the paper’s projection formula. It neither constructs a spatial field nor states the full projection identity.
e01.conventions.leray-projection.TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode_zero: The formal theorem proves that the scalar correction’s zero Fourier coefficient vanishes, fixing the mean of the potential. The paper additionally gives the full identity for the Leray projection. The single zero-mode statement does not establish that identity and does not remove the constant part of velocity.

e01.conventions.pressure-normalization.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution: For a smooth periodic Euler solution on $[0,T_*)$, the formal condition requires $\int_{[-1/2,1/2]^3}p(t,x)\,dx=0$ at each $0\le t<T_*$. The cube has volume one, so this is exactly zero spatial mean on $\mathbb T^3$. Adding an arbitrary function of time to the pressure would preserve its gradient but generally violate this normalization. The condition concerns the solution interval only.

e01.conventions.periodic-flow-displaceme.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.add_latticeVect: For a periodic velocity on a closed time interval, uniformly Lipschitz in space with one constant, and a flow satisfying its trajectory and initial conditions, the formal theorem states $X(s,t,x+n)=X(s,t,x)+n$ for every integer vector $n$ and times in the interval. Subtracting $x+n$ gives periodic lifted displacement. Smooth periodic parents on the compact time interval meet the regularity used for this convention.

r2a1.intro.derivative-conventions.TorusEuler.divergence: The paper specifies the full gradient convention and rowwise divergence of a matrix field. The linked definition gives only $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_i\partial_i v_i$ for a differentiable vector field. It is compatible with the diagonal trace convention, but does not itself define all matrix-gradient entries or rowwise matrix divergence. At nondifferentiable points the derivative expression is assigned zero, so classical use requires the separate regularity assumptions.

r5-root-schedule-purpose.TorusEuler.paperTheorem71: The formal theorem constructs a scheduled sequence with residual bounds, localized oscillations of size at most $\lambda_j^{-1}$, and corrections bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1}$ through the retained orders. Fast growth of frequencies and increasing retained orders give the summability used in the introduction. Those summability deductions are not stated explicitly in this theorem, and it does not separately attribute the estimates to every individual truncation term.
r5-root-schedule-purpose.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: For a given sequence, the formal conditions impose small oscillations and spatial Hölder corrections on the whole stage interval, and vanishing of later oscillations through activation. They quantify the effects described in the paper, but are assumptions on a construction rather than a proof that a chosen frequency schedule realizes them or that the resulting series converges.

e01.parameters.exponent.TorusEuler.frequencyExponent: The paper defines $K(s)=320b(s+1)$ for integers $s\ge1$, with $b\ge1$ fixed. The formal formula uses the same integer expression for all nonnegative integers $b,s$, including zero. On the paper’s parameter range it agrees exactly; its broader domain is a convention and supplies no positivity assumption when $b=0$.

e01.parameters.monotone-threshold.TorusEuler.fixedOrderThreshold: The paper permits any nondecreasing positive threshold satisfying its cost and logarithmic bounds. The formal definition chooses a particular candidate: the maximum of $e^{4K(s+1)^3}$ and a finite sum of absolute costs up to order and depth $7K(s)$. The formula itself does not assert monotonicity; a separate theorem proves it.
e01.parameters.monotone-threshold.TorusEuler.fixedOrderThreshold_mono: For the explicit threshold formed from the exponential floor and the finite absolute-cost sum, the formal theorem proves monotonicity on all nonnegative integers, including zero. The paper requires it only on positive integers. No monotonicity of the individual costs is assumed.
e01.parameters.monotone-threshold.TorusEuler.Paper.AdmissibleThreshold: The paper asks for a choice of threshold with the required properties. The formal condition asks a given $\mathcal B$ to be nondecreasing on positive integers, positive, above a proposed majorant $F$, and above the logarithmic floor. It does not construct such a function or establish that $F$ bounds the analytic constants.

e01.parameters.cost-domination.TorusEuler.abs_fixedOrderCost_le_thresho: The paper requires domination of all fixed-order analytic constants through order and depth $7K(s)$. The formal theorem bounds every entry of any supplied finite cost table by its explicit threshold, including zero orders and depths. This proves the finite-sum domination, but identifying that table with all the analytic constants is a separate step, not a conclusion of this theorem.
e01.parameters.cost-domination.TorusEuler.Paper.AdmissibleThreshold: The formal condition requires only $F(s)\le\mathcal B(s)$ for a supplied majorant $F$, alongside positivity, monotonicity and the logarithmic floor. The paper’s claim is that $\mathcal B(s)$ dominates the actual analytic constants. That conclusion needs a separate identification and bound for $F$; it is not encoded by the inequality alone.

e01.parameters.log-floor.TorusEuler.fixedOrderThreshold_log_floor: For the explicitly chosen threshold, the formal theorem gives $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$ for every nonnegative integer $s$ and $b$. The paper uses $s\ge1$ and $b\ge1$. Positivity follows from the exponential term in that particular threshold, so no extension convention for the logarithm is involved.
e01.parameters.log-floor.TorusEuler.Paper.AdmissibleThreshold: The admissibility condition imposes exactly the floor (1.13) at every positive integer $s$, with a separate requirement $\mathcal B(s)>0$. It records a hypothesis on the chosen threshold. It does not prove that an arbitrary function satisfies it.

e01.parameters.initial-frequency.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters: The formal parameter conditions require $\mathcal B(1)\le\lambda_0$. Identifying $N=\lambda_0$ gives exactly the initial-frequency inequality in the paper. Here $\lambda_0$ is real, whereas the orders $q_j$ and the separation exponents are nonnegative integers. This inequality constrains supplied parameters. It does not construct a frequency sequence or any Euler velocity.

e01.parameters.initial-order.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters: The formal parameter conditions require the nonnegative-integer sequence $q$ to satisfy $q_1=1$. The maximum rule then determines $q_2,q_3,\ldots$ using the preceding frequencies and the threshold. No value of $q_0$ is prescribed by this initial-order clause. Thus the paper and the formal statement start the derivative-order sequence at the same index.

e01.parameters.schedule.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_exists: The formal theorem constructs $q_j,\lambda_j$ satisfying $q_1=1$, $\lambda_0=N$, the frequency recurrence and the maximum rule, assuming $b\ge1$, $N\ge1$ and $\mathcal B(1)\le N$. It does not define $\Lambda_j,L_j,\varepsilon_j$ or prove their bounds. These are separate parts of the displayed schedule.
e01.parameters.schedule.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters: The formal parameter conditions record $q_1=1$, the recurrence and maximum rule, positivity and the logarithmic threshold floor. They do not contain the entire display: the cutoff frequencies, logarithmic gains and coupling ratios are defined elsewhere. They also omit threshold monotonicity and cost domination, and assert no existence by themselves.
e01.parameters.schedule.TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.L: This formal definition gives exactly $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$ for a supplied real frequency sequence. It defines only the gain part of (1.14), not the recurrence or maximum rule. Under the paper’s frequencies $\lambda_j>1$, the gains are positive.
e01.parameters.schedule.TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.ε: This formal definition gives $\varepsilon_j=L_{j+1}^{-2}$, which is (1.14) after shifting the index. It also assigns a value at the unused index zero and assigns zero if the gain is zero. The paper uses positive gains and $j\ge1$. The other parts of the schedule are not stated here.

e01.parameters.arbitrary-threshold-growt.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_order_tends: Assuming $q_1=1$, $\mathcal B(1)\le\lambda_0$, the maximum rule, and nondecreasing frequencies tending to infinity, the formal theorem proves $q_j\to\infty$. There is no monotonicity, positivity or growth-rate restriction on the threshold. Thus the arithmetic conclusion applies more generally than the schedule in §1.5, but frequency divergence remains an explicit assumption.

e01.lemma13.orders.TorusEuler.paperLemma13_slowOrders: As the preceding frequency grows, an order already admitted by its threshold stays available for the next maximum. The cap on that maximum allows an increase of at most one. When the frequencies tend to infinity, every fixed order eventually becomes attainable.
e01.lemma13.orders.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_1_3: The hypothesis written `IsGreatest` selects the largest order whose threshold fits the preceding frequency and whose value is at most $q_j+1$. The conclusion bounds the change at each step and separately gives divergence of the whole order sequence.
e01.lemma13.orders.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_1_3: The named theorem gives a single schedule two properties used in the later construction. Consecutive allowed orders differ by at most one, and each fixed derivative order is eventually allowed. The finite step estimates and the limiting smoothness argument use those properties at different points.
e01.lemma13.orders.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_1_3: The proof calls the schedule theorem with index $i=j-1$ to turn the paper's first positive stage into $i=0$. It takes the successive-order inequalities from that theorem at index $i$ and reuses convergence of the same full order sequence directly.

e01.lemma13.logarithmic-bound.TorusEuler.paperLemma13_slowOrders: The later logarithm equals the earlier logarithm times three successive frequency exponents. The threshold floor was chosen to dominate four times that product even if the order rises at both intervening steps. Multiplying by the earlier logarithm gives the square on the right.
e01.lemma13.logarithmic-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_1_3: Here `Schedule.L freq (j + 1)` is $4\log\lambda_{j+2}$. The last clause states the comparison with $\log^2\lambda_{j-1}$ for every positive $j$. The paper uses this to pay for a coming wave's gain using a preceding frequency.
e01.lemma13.logarithmic-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_1_3: The numbered theorem packages the logarithmic bound in the paper's stage indices. It is available to later stage estimates as $L_{j+1}\le(\log\lambda_{j-1})^2$, so any fixed power of this gain can eventually be absorbed by a positive power of the preceding frequency.
e01.lemma13.logarithmic-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_1_3: In the last proof branch, take $j=i+1$ and unfold `Schedule.L`. This turns the desired left side into four times the logarithm of `freq (i + 3)` and the right side into the square of the logarithm of `freq i`. The core log bound then applies directly.

r2a1.wave.self-advection.TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection: Under $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$ and differentiability of $F$ at $k\cdot x$, the formal statement proves the final equality $(w\cdot\nabla)w=0$. r2a1.wave.pressure-gradient.TorusEuler.hasGradientAt_affineWavePress: The formal statement gives $\nabla p=-Sx-p_{\rm w}F(k\cdot x)k$ under symmetry of $S$ and $P'=F$ at the phase. Identifying the second acceleration term with $p_{\rm w}kF$ still requires the amplitude equation, which is not a hypothesis or conclusion of this spatial-gradient identity.

r2a1.wave.divergence.TorusEuler.divergence_affineWaveVelocity: The formal statement proves $\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{tr}D+(k\cdot\mathbf a)F'$ for a profile differentiable at the phase. affine.pairing-cancellation.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_affineWavePa: For an arbitrary coefficient $p_{\rm w}$, the formal statement proves only $(k\cdot\mathbf a)'=-2k\cdot D\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}|k|^2$. affine.wave-vector-nonvanishing.TorusEuler.linearODE_ne_zero_of_mem: Take the operator in the linear ODE to be $-D(t)^T$. If the wave vector were zero at any time, uniqueness with that zero value would force the solution to be zero also at $t_0$. The theorem applies to continuous bounded-linear coefficients on the interval.

affine.linear-amplitude-equation.TorusEuler.affineWaveAmplitudeOperator: The paper states an evolution equation. The formal definition gives its linear right-hand-side operator $\mathbf a\mapsto-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$, equivalent to the displayed projection formula when $k\ne0$. It does not assert that any path has this derivative. The wave-equation condition supplies that assumption. At $k=0$ the operator is defined as $-D$.

affine.amplitude-nonvanishing.TorusEuler.linearODE_ne_zero_of_mem: Once the wave vector stays nonzero, the factor $1/|k(t)|^2$ in the amplitude equation is continuous. r5-reference-small-ratio-gain.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, let $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ and consider $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)Y-Y^2$, $Y(0)=1$, on $[0,\infty)$. The formal statement proves the whole assertion of Lemma 2.5, including uniqueness for all $\tau\ge0$.
